people.name: Anneke Vos
people.role: historian of cartography who studied survey field notebooks

people.name: Efosa Delgado
people.role: geographer who compared old triangulation points with satellite positions

people.name: Shirin Farouk
people.role: researcher who studies volunteer mapping projects

paragraphs.text: Until well into the twentieth century, a detailed map of a country began with people walking across it. Surveyors carried measuring chains, heavy brass instruments and notebooks, and they depended on triangulation, a technique borrowed from geometry. A team would first measure a single straight line on flat ground, called a baseline, with great care, sometimes over several weeks. From each end of this line they sighted a distant landmark, such as a church tower or a hilltop, and recorded the angles. Because one side and two angles are enough to fix the rest of a triangle, the surveyors could calculate distances they had never walked, then use each new side as the starting point for another triangle. In this way a chain of triangles gradually spread across the landscape.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The method was accurate but painfully slow. Large national surveys in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries took decades to complete, and survey parties endured heat, disease and harsh weather while hauling equipment up hills. Yet according to Anneke Vos, a historian of cartography, the physical hardship is only part of the story. After studying the field notebooks of several surveys, she argues that the finished maps concealed countless small decisions: which villages to record, whose spelling of a place name to adopt, and which paths were important enough to draw. Some of these choices, she adds, were made by surveyors who did not speak the local language. 'A map looks like a neutral picture,' she writes, 'but every line on it was chosen by someone standing in a particular place.'
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: The first great acceleration came from the air. After the First World War, cameras mounted in aircraft were used to photograph large areas in overlapping strips. Specialists then examined pairs of these images through stereoscopes, instruments that made the ground appear three-dimensional and allowed the height of hills and valleys to be measured. This technique, known as photogrammetry, did not abolish fieldwork – someone still had to visit the ground to name features and check fixed points – but it reduced the walking dramatically. Aerial photographs also captured details, such as the precise outline of a coastline or the edge of a forest, that a surveyor on foot could easily misjudge. A district that might once have occupied a survey party for several seasons could now be photographed in a few days.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Satellites changed the scale once again. From 1972, satellites designed to study the Earth's surface began sending back regular images of almost every part of the planet, allowing map-makers to track changes such as spreading cities, retreating glaciers and new roads. Later, satellite navigation systems let anyone with a receiver work out their position by timing signals from several satellites at once. For years civilian users received a deliberately degraded signal, but in 2000 this restriction was switched off, and ordinary receivers became accurate to within a few metres. Efosa Delgado, a geographer who compared old triangulation points with their modern satellite positions, found that many nineteenth-century measurements were out by less than a metre. He attributes this not to the quality of the surveyors' instruments but to their habit of repeating every angle many times and averaging the results.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Perhaps the deepest change, however, lies not in how information is collected but in how it is stored. A printed map is a finished object; once the ink is dry, correcting it means printing a new edition. Digital mapping systems instead keep information in separate layers – roads, rivers, buildings, land use – that can be combined, updated or hidden at will. This has made maps far cheaper to revise, but it has also shifted the main problem from gathering information to managing it. Shirin Farouk, who studies volunteer mapping projects, notes that thousands of unpaid contributors now add streets and buildings to online maps. In her research on one coastal region, volunteers recorded footpaths and small shops that appeared on no government map. She also found, however, that coverage was uneven: wealthy urban districts were mapped in fine detail, while poorer rural areas received far less attention.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: The way people use maps has changed as well. Pavel Kimura, who researches human navigation, asked two groups of walkers to cross an unfamiliar town, one following turn-by-turn directions on a phone and the other using a paper map. Those guided by the phone arrived slightly sooner and made fewer wrong turns, but when asked afterwards to sketch their route, they produced far less accurate drawings. Kimura suggests that when a device takes over the work of orientation, people pay less attention to landmarks, although he cautions that his study involved only short journeys.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: For all these changes, some things remain remarkably constant. Satellite positions are still checked against fixed markers on the ground, and map-makers continue to face the questions that troubled their predecessors: what to include, what to leave out and what to call it. The tools have moved from the hillside into orbit, but the judgement behind every map is still a human one.
paragraphs.label: G

section.text:
From Chains to Satellites

A. Until well into the twentieth century, a detailed map of a country began with people walking across it. Surveyors carried measuring chains, heavy brass instruments and notebooks, and they depended on triangulation, a technique borrowed from geometry. A team would first measure a single straight line on flat ground, called a baseline, with great care, sometimes over several weeks. From each end of this line they sighted a distant landmark, such as a church tower or a hilltop, and recorded the angles. Because one side and two angles are enough to fix the rest of a triangle, the surveyors could calculate distances they had never walked, then use each new side as the starting point for another triangle. In this way a chain of triangles gradually spread across the landscape.

B. The method was accurate but painfully slow. Large national surveys in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries took decades to complete, and survey parties endured heat, disease and harsh weather while hauling equipment up hills. Yet according to Anneke Vos, a historian of cartography, the physical hardship is only part of the story. After studying the field notebooks of several surveys, she argues that the finished maps concealed countless small decisions: which villages to record, whose spelling of a place name to adopt, and which paths were important enough to draw. Some of these choices, she adds, were made by surveyors who did not speak the local language. 'A map looks like a neutral picture,' she writes, 'but every line on it was chosen by someone standing in a particular place.'

C. The first great acceleration came from the air. After the First World War, cameras mounted in aircraft were used to photograph large areas in overlapping strips. Specialists then examined pairs of these images through stereoscopes, instruments that made the ground appear three-dimensional and allowed the height of hills and valleys to be measured. This technique, known as photogrammetry, did not abolish fieldwork – someone still had to visit the ground to name features and check fixed points – but it reduced the walking dramatically. Aerial photographs also captured details, such as the precise outline of a coastline or the edge of a forest, that a surveyor on foot could easily misjudge. A district that might once have occupied a survey party for several seasons could now be photographed in a few days.

D. Satellites changed the scale once again. From 1972, satellites designed to study the Earth's surface began sending back regular images of almost every part of the planet, allowing map-makers to track changes such as spreading cities, retreating glaciers and new roads. Later, satellite navigation systems let anyone with a receiver work out their position by timing signals from several satellites at once. For years civilian users received a deliberately degraded signal, but in 2000 this restriction was switched off, and ordinary receivers became accurate to within a few metres. Efosa Delgado, a geographer who compared old triangulation points with their modern satellite positions, found that many nineteenth-century measurements were out by less than a metre. He attributes this not to the quality of the surveyors' instruments but to their habit of repeating every angle many times and averaging the results.

E. Perhaps the deepest change, however, lies not in how information is collected but in how it is stored. A printed map is a finished object; once the ink is dry, correcting it means printing a new edition. Digital mapping systems instead keep information in separate layers – roads, rivers, buildings, land use – that can be combined, updated or hidden at will. This has made maps far cheaper to revise, but it has also shifted the main problem from gathering information to managing it. Shirin Farouk, who studies volunteer mapping projects, notes that thousands of unpaid contributors now add streets and buildings to online maps. In her research on one coastal region, volunteers recorded footpaths and small shops that appeared on no government map. She also found, however, that coverage was uneven: wealthy urban districts were mapped in fine detail, while poorer rural areas received far less attention.

F. The way people use maps has changed as well. Pavel Kimura, who researches human navigation, asked two groups of walkers to cross an unfamiliar town, one following turn-by-turn directions on a phone and the other using a paper map. Those guided by the phone arrived slightly sooner and made fewer wrong turns, but when asked afterwards to sketch their route, they produced far less accurate drawings. Kimura suggests that when a device takes over the work of orientation, people pay less attention to landmarks, although he cautions that his study involved only short journeys.

G. For all these changes, some things remain remarkably constant. Satellite positions are still checked against fixed markers on the ground, and map-makers continue to face the questions that troubled their predecessors: what to include, what to leave out and what to call it. The tools have moved from the hillside into orbit, but the judgement behind every map is still a human one.
